* # [PHOENIX-7490](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PHOENIX-7490): Lookup for tenant PTable returns global PTable

## Background

Phoenix has a metadata cache on the client side which is used by queries, upserts and deletes. The metadata cache is per ConnectionQueryServices object and is shared by all Phoenix connections using the same ConnectionQueryServices object. The metadata cache is implemented using the PMetadataImpl class. The metadata cache uses PTableKey as the key in cache for storing PTableRef. PTableKey has tenant Id (if the corresponding PTableRef object is tenant specific) and full name of the table/view/index. The tenant Id in PTableKey will be the same as the tenant Id of the tenant connection used for creating tenant view or tenant view index or it will be null.

Phoenix first tries to lookup a PTable object in client metadata cache and if can’t find it there or it’s age is more than configured max age of an object in the cache then looks it up in SYSCAT metadata cache (which can eventually end up doing a SYSCAT scan if PTable object is not even in SYSCAT metadata cache).

When we query, we call MetaDataClient\#updateCache() to get the PTableRef object corresponding to the table in the FROM clause of the query. This method first looks up the PTableRef object in the metadata cache. If we are using a tenant connection then first tenant specific PTableRef object is looked up in the metadata cache and if it is not found then the global PTableRef object is looked up. Finally, depending on the value of UCF a lookup is done in SYSCAT metadata cache to get latest PTable object but if we already found a global PTableRef object in client metadata cache then even while looking up in SYSCAT metadata cache we will only lookup the latest global PTable object. Thus, even though we are using tenant connection we never even try to lookup in SYSCAT metadata cache if there is a PTable object corresponding to the tenant. As a result we end up querying the global table when we intended to query the tenant view\!\!

When we upsert, we call PhoenixConnection\#getTable() as part of Statement\#executeUpdate() to get a PTable object for the table to which we want to upsert. When using tenant connection we first try to get PTableRef from metadata cache but if not found then we call MetaDataClient\#updateCache() with alwaysHitServer as true (implying we will certainly hit SYSCAT RS). But if the metadata cache contains PTableRef for global object and not for tenant object then we will hit SYSCAT RS to lookup metadata for global PTable object. Thus, if we are using tenant connection and PTableRef for tenant object is not in the metadata cache but PTableRef of global object is in metadata cache then we will end up inserting row in global table while we intended to insert row in tenant view\!\!

## Problem Statement

When a tenant view and global table have same name, we are using tenant connection and PTableRef object of tenant view is not in metadata cache but PTableRef object of global table is in metadata cache then we can end up inserting rows in global table and querying rows from global table while the intention is to use tenant view.

## Design Principle

1. Data should be inserted into/queried from the intended table/view/index.  
2. There should be no performance regression for use cases where a tenant view and a global table won’t have the same name.

## Solution

When using tenant connection the following sequence of events should happen when trying to get a PTable object. 

1. Lookup in metadata cache for tenant specific PTableRef object. If found we are good.  
2. If no PTable object is found in the metadata cache then do a lookup in SYSCAT metadata cache (which might eventually do a lookup in SYSCAT if needed). If a PTable object is found in the SYSCAT metadata cache then we are good.  
3. If no PTable object is found then lookup for global object in the metadata cache. If found then we are good.  
4. If no PTable object is found then lookup for global object in SYSCAT metadata cache. If found we are good.  
5. If no PTable object is found then throw TableNotFoundException.

Currently, step2 is not being done. We are going to step 3 after step 1 and due to that even when using tenant connection and intending to insert/query the tenant view, we are inserting rows in/querying rows from global table. 

If we start doing step 2, then for the cases when we are using tenant connection to upsert/query multi-tenant global table then we will end up doing an RPC call to SYSCAT RS always. To optimize this we can introduce a “Negative Tenant Cache” (referred to as NTC in the rest of the doc). 

NTC will be at ConnectionQueryServices level. The keys of this cache will be PTableKey objects with tenant Id as non-null. If there is an entry in cache with PTableKey having tenant Id as “tenant1” and name as “table1” then that means there is no tenant specific PTable object in SYSCAT for tenantId: “tenant1” and table name: “table1”. Thus, this new cache can be used to avoid doing repeated lookups to SYSCAT metadata cache when there is no tenant specific PTable object with the given name even in SYSCAT. 

An entry in NTC will imply there is no PTable object for the specific tenant with the given table/view/index name in SYSCAT. But we should also have a frequency at which entries in NTC will be invalidated like how we have UPDATE\_CACHE\_FERQUENCY for existing metadata cache. We can call this new config as “phoenix.default.update.negative.cache.frequency” (UCF of NTC). This config will define the max age of an entry in NTC. If an entry in NTC has age less than “phoenix.default.update.negative.cache.frequency” then RPC to SYSCAT RS will be skipped like how UPDATE\_CACHE\_FREQUENCY is used to skip RPC to SYSCAT RS based on age of PTableRef object. 

## Final Solution with NTC 

Lookup tenant object using tenant connection

![][image1]

When using tenant connection and looking up a tenant object, following steps will be followed:

1. Check for tenant object’s PTableRef in client metadata cache.  
2. If the tenant object is found in the client metadata cache then compare its age with UCF.  
   1. If the age of the tenant object in client metadata cache is less than UCF then we return the PTable object.  
   2. If the age of the tenant object in the client metadata cache is greater than or equal to UCF then we make a call to SYSCAT RS to lookup the tenant object. Steps taken during the call to SYSCAT RS are explained in subsequent diagrams.  
3. If the tenant object is not found in client metadata cache the lookup for entry of tenant object in NTC.   
4. If an entry for tenant object is found in NTC then compare its age with UCF of NTC.  
   1. If the age of entry for the tenant object in NTC is less than UCF of NTC then we lookup for a global object with the same name as the tenant object. This case signifies that NTC is telling us that there is no tenant object with the given name and we should try looking up for the global object. Steps taken during looking up global object are explained in subsequent diagrams.  
   2. If the age of entry for the tenant object in NTC is greater than or equal to UCF of NTC then we make a call to SYSCAT RS to lookup the tenant object. Steps taken during the call to SYSCAT RS are explained in subsequent diagrams.  
5. If no entry is found for the tenant object in NTC then we make a call to SYSCAT RS to lookup the tenant object. Steps taken during the call to SYSCAT RS are explained in subsequent diagrams.

Lookup global object using tenant or global connection  
![][image2]  
When looking up a global object, following steps will be followed:

1. Check for global object’s PTableRef in client metadata cache.  
2. If the global object is found in the client metadata cache then compare its age with UCF.  
   1. If the age of the global object in client metadata cache is less than UCF then we check if the Phoenix connection is a tenant connection or a global connection.  
      1. If the connection type is a tenant connection, then add an entry to NTC. The addition of an entry to NTC will end up updating if an entry already exists but its age is \>= UCF of NTC. Finally return the global PTable object. This signifies that there is a global object but no tenant object with the given name.  
      2. If the connection type is global connection then return global PTable object.  
   2. If the age of the tenant object in the client metadata cache is greater than or equal to UCF then we make a call to SYSCAT RS to lookup global object. Steps taken during the call to SYSCAT RS are explained in subsequent diagrams.  
3. If the global object is not found in the client metadata cache then make a call to SYSCAT RS to lookup the global object. Steps taken during the call to SYSCAT RS are explained in subsequent diagrams.

Lookup tenant and global objects from SYSCAT metadata cache  
![][image3]  
When looking up tenant and global object in SYSCAT metadata cache, following steps will be followed:

1. Make a RPC call to SYSCAT RS to lookup Phoenix object (tenant/global) in SYSCAT metadata cache.  
2. If the Phoenix object is found in SYSCAT metadata cache (or read from SYSCAT) then cache it in client metadata cache. Check the connection type being used by the client and type of object we are looking up i.e. tenant or global.  
   1. If we are looking up a global object using the tenant connection then add an entry to NTC for the tenant object as we know the tenant object is not there in SYSCAT but the global object is there. Finally return the PTable object.   
   2. If we are looking up a tenant object using the tenant connection then evict entry for the tenant object from NTC as we did find the tenant object in SYSCAT. Finally return the PTable object.   
   3. If we are looking up a global object using global connection then return PTable object.  
3. If the Phoenix object is not found in SYSCAT then check which type of Phoenix object we were looking for i.e. tenant or global.  
   1. If we were looking up tenant object then:  
      1. Evict tenant object from client metadata cache as we know tenant object is not there even in SYSCAT.  
      2. Invoke lookup for global object. Steps taken during looking up global object are explained in the above diagram.  
   2. If we were looking up global object then:  
      1. Evict entry for tenant object from NTC as we know there is no Phoenix object with the given name. Neither a tenant object nor a global object exists with the given name in SYSCAT. This needs to be done only if we were using tenant connection.  
      2. Evict global object from client metadata cache.  
      3. Throw TNFE as there is no Phoenix object with the given name\!\!

Eviction from NTC apart from shown in above diagrams

Entry will be evicted from NTC if any of the following conditions are met:

1. Due to the size of NTC reaching its max and entries have to be evicted.  
   1. Maximum size of NTC will be configurable via config: “phoenix.client.maxNegativeCacheSize”. This will specify the max size of NTC in bytes.  
   2. The default value can be 10MB like how we have for existing metadata cache.   
   3. Each entry in this cache will be small as we will be storing PTableKey and a constant empty Optional object as key/value pair.  
2. A tenant view or a tenant view index is created with the same PTableKey as an entry in NTC.  
   1. The entry will be evicted from the cache corresponding to the CQSI used for tenant view/view index creation.
